Being superalert or watchful or on guard

vignette:
Kwame Osei, a 33-year-old Ghanaian-American tailor, sat in the shop he had built from nothing, his hands steady on a bolt of charcoal wool, his eyes fixed on the door. It was a habit he could no longer suppress—every time the bell jingled, he mapped the distance to the exit, noted the angle of the counter, calculated whether he could slip past a customer if he needed to. Three years had passed since the bombing, but his body still behaved as though the next explosion was seconds away.

The attack had happened on a Tuesday, during the evening rush at the downtown transit hub. Kwame had been on his way home after delivering a custom suit to a client. He remembered the crush of commuters, the stale heat underground, the flickering fluorescent lights. Then the world folded into a roar that seemed to come from inside his skull. He remembered nothing of the next several minutes—only waking on the platform floor, ears ringing, a gash on his forearm, people screaming and running. The police later told him a man had detonated a vest. Kwame’s memory held only fragments: a blurred image of a woman’s shoe lying alone, the smell of burnt metal, the strange whiteness of the smoke. The gaps unsettled him more than the images that did come, because he could never be sure what he had seen and what his mind had invented.

In the months afterward, Kwame found he could recall the event with almost photographic clarity—but only when he did not want to. The film would start without warning: the pressure wave, the shatter of glass, the woman’s shoe. Other times, he could describe the whole thing to a friend or a therapist (he saw one briefly) and feel nothing, as though he were reciting a story about someone else. That numbness frightened him more than the fear did. If he could feel nothing about something so terrible, what kind of person was he?

That question became a shadow that followed him everywhere. He had always thought of himself as capable, as someone others could rely on. But after the bombing, doubt crept into every decision. Could he trust his own instincts? He had frozen during the attack—stood there, stunned, while others ran—and he had turned that moment over in his mind a thousand times. A strong person would have helped someone, would have done something. Instead, he had been useless. He became certain that he was weak, and that everyone who knew what had happened must see it too. He stopped going to the neighborhood gatherings he had once enjoyed. He stopped returning calls from his cousins. The feeling that he no longer belonged anywhere settled into his chest like a permanent cold.

At work, he made his shop a fortress. He moved his cutting table so his back faced the wall and he could see the entire room. He kept the door slightly ajar so he could hear the street. Whenever a customer walked in, he scanned them from head to toe, looking for anything unusual—a bulky coat, a nervous hand. He began picking arguments with clients over small mistakes in their orders, or with the delivery driver who was five minutes late. The fights made his heart race, but they also pushed away the intrusive images for an hour or two. The relief never lasted, and afterward he felt even more alone.

His evenings became a blur of phone games and streaming videos, hours lost in scrolling because stillness meant thinking. He could not make plans for the future—not for a vacation, not for the next weekend, not even for a dentist appointment. Every time he tried, a voice inside him whispered that there was no point, that something would happen to upend it anyway. So he lived day to day, drifting through his work, avoiding the weight of tomorrow.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a moment of quiet terror. He had been sitting in his shop after closing, phone in hand, when he realized he had spent four hours doing nothing—not even scrolling, just staring at the screen, waiting for the next day to start. He had stopped making eye contact with his own reflection. He was afraid that if he kept going this way, he would shrink until he disappeared entirely. He did not know if therapy could fix the memory gaps or the hypervigilance or the certainty that he was worthless. But he knew he could not spend another year hiding behind a wall, waiting for the next explosion.
